11.3 — Written-Response Practice (PPR in hand)

The exam's written section gives you 60 minutes for 4 prompts, and the only notes allowed are the PPR you built (11.2a). Today you rehearse the real conditions: prompts unseen, PPR in hand, clock running — and you learn the sentence shapes the rubrics reward.

Drill One ~25 min

The exam-day WR structure (different from your PT prompts — see the full guide):

  • WR1: a NEW program you read — identify/describe behavior, input, output (not your own program!)
  • WR2a/2b/2c: YOUR program, with your PPR: algorithm explanation, list usage, and development difficulty + fix
  • WR on a provided code excerpt: reading/analyzing code you have never seen

The shapes that score:

  1. Claim + evidence + because: "The procedure returns -1 when the list is empty BECAUSE the loop never executes and the initial value of total is returned."
  2. Name the mechanism, not the vibe: "sequencing because lines 2→3 depend on each other" beats "it does things in order."
  3. For your PPR answers: quote your own variable names. "my inventory list" scores; "my list" scores less.

Drill (15 minutes, timed): with your PPR printed and in hand, write WR2a (algorithm) and WR2c (list) from scratch, exam-paper style. Swap with a partner: does THEIR rubric read (does the evidence quote real code lines) hold up? Full rubrics on the guide page.

Bug Hunt: WR losing points

  1. Answer describes what the code "should" do rather than what it DOES. Why does the rubric language always ask about the code AS SUBMITTED?
  2. WR2b says "I struggled with errors and fixed them." Which three things are missing (specific bug, specific cause, specific fix — the rubric names all three)?
  3. You write a beautiful answer about your list... that contradicts your PPR's actual code. Which document does the grader check against which?
Drill Two ~20 min

Read code cold (the WR1 skill). Here is a foreign program, exam-style — describe its behavior in three sentences or fewer:

PROCEDURE mystery(list, target)
{
    count ← 0
    FOR EACH item IN list
    {
        IF (item > target)
        {
            count ← count + 1
        }
    }
    RETURN count
}

Write: input (___ and ___), behavior (___), output (___). Then the graders' follow-up style: what does mystery(list, 0) return for a list of all negative numbers? What about an empty list — trace the loop count.

Tinker: Your turn to write prompts

  1. Write YOUR OWN two exam-style questions: one pseudocode trace, one "identify the error" (like 1.3's bug hunts — you have been training this since September). Swap with a partner and grade each other with the sentence shapes as the rubric.
  2. Commit your drills: "11.3a: WR drills".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Write claim+evidence answers quoting real variable names
  • Describe foreign code's input/behavior/output in 3 sentences
  • Answer WR2b with the specific bug-cause-fix triple
  • Finish a timed WR2a+2c drill inside 15 minutes
